title: Pre-emptive Pharmacogenomic Testing in Health Systems
text_chunk: Pre-emptive pharmacogenomic testing genotypes patients before an actionable prescription is written, storing results in the EHR for future clinical decision support. The Vanderbilt PREDICT program (established 2010) was the first large-scale pre-emptive PGx implementation, genotyping >35,000 patients with results embedded in the electronic health record. Key success factors include: (1) test-once, use-many-times model — a single multi-gene PGx test costs $200-500 but provides lifetime value; (2) automated CDS alerts at point-of-prescribing; (3) clinical pharmacist review of alerts; (4) provider education program. Cost-effectiveness analyses show pre-emptive testing becomes cost-saving when patients encounter >=2 actionable prescriptions over their lifetime.
outcomes: 35,000+ patients genotyped; 60% reduction in adverse cardiovascular events with CYP2C19-guided clopidogrel; 72% provider alert acceptance rate

institution: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital PG4KDS
title: EHR-Integrated Pharmacogenomic Clinical Decision Support
text_chunk: Electronic health record (EHR) integration is critical for actionable PGx implementation. The St. Jude PG4KDS (Pharmacogenomics for Kids) program established best practices: (1) Structured discrete data storage of genotype results (not free-text); (2) Automated translation of genotype to phenotype using standardized CPIC definitions; (3) Interruptive CDS alerts for high-risk drug-gene interactions (e.g., codeine in CYP2D6 UM); (4) Passive CDS (information banners) for moderate-risk interactions; (5) Pre-calculated phenotype display in patient chart for quick reference. Technical requirements include HL7 FHIR-compatible PGx result messaging, standardized terminology (LOINC codes for PGx results), and CDS rule maintenance as guidelines evolve.
outcomes: All St. Jude patients (~5000/year) receive pre-emptive PGx testing; 95% alert uptime; <0.1% false positive rate for high-risk CDS alerts

title: Reactive (Point-of-Care) Pharmacogenomic Testing Workflows
text_chunk: Reactive PGx testing is ordered at the time of prescribing, with results returned before or shortly after drug initiation. This approach requires rapid turnaround time (ideally <24 hours, optimally <2 hours for urgent situations like PCI). Rapid genotyping platforms include: (1) Spartan Bioscience CYP2C19 RX (buccal swab, 60-minute turnaround); (2) GenMark ePlex (multiplex, 90 minutes); (3) ID NOW-style LAMP assays (under development). Advantages: no upfront testing cost for patients who may never need an actionable drug. Disadvantages: potential delay in urgent therapy, missed opportunities for pre-emptive alerts, lower test utilization. Reactive testing is most practical for CYP2C19/clopidogrel at the cardiac catheterization lab and DPYD/fluoropyrimidines before chemotherapy initiation.
outcomes: Point-of-care CYP2C19 testing feasible in 95% of PCI cases; results available before cath lab discharge in 87% of patients

title: Clinical Decision Support Alert Design for Pharmacogenomics
text_chunk: Effective PGx CDS alert design must balance clinical impact with alert fatigue. Consensus recommendations from the IGNITE Network and CPIC: (1) Tiered alert severity: HARD STOP (contraindication, e.g., abacavir + HLA-B*57:01), INTERRUPTIVE (high risk requiring acknowledgment, e.g., codeine + CYP2D6 UM), PASSIVE (informational banner, e.g., statin + SLCO1B1 heterozygote). (2) Actionable content: specific alternative drugs and doses, not just warnings. (3) Override documentation: require reason when overriding high-risk alerts. (4) Context-sensitive firing: suppress alerts for established/chronic medications unless dose change. (5) Pharmacist co-signature for complex PGx decisions. Alert acceptance rates: hard stops 95%, interruptive 60-75%, passive 30-50%.
outcomes: Tiered alert design reduces alert fatigue from >90% override rate to 25-40% override rate for appropriately classified alerts

title: Provider Education and Training for Pharmacogenomics Implementation
text_chunk: Provider education is consistently identified as the #1 barrier to PGx implementation. Key strategies: (1) Just-in-time education: brief, focused educational content delivered within the CDS alert itself (what the result means, what to do, why); (2) Grand rounds and CME programs: periodic case-based education for physicians and pharmacists; (3) PGx clinical pharmacist consultation service: available for complex multi-gene interpretation; (4) Standardized competencies: ASHP and ACCP have published PGx competency frameworks for pharmacy education; (5) Patient-facing materials: multilingual educational resources explaining PGx test results. Surveys show that while >90% of providers believe PGx is important, only 10-20% feel adequately trained to interpret results, highlighting the education-implementation gap.
outcomes: Just-in-time education increases alert acceptance by 15-20%; dedicated PGx pharmacist consultation improves genotype-concordant prescribing from 55% to 82%

title: Recommended Pharmacogenomic Testing Panels
text_chunk: Multi-gene PGx testing panels vary by clinical context: CORE PANEL (minimum 7 genes): CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, DPYD, TPMT, NUDT15, SLCO1B1. Covers the majority of CPIC Level A drug-gene pairs. COMPREHENSIVE PANEL (12-15 genes): adds CYP3A5, CYP2B6, CYP1A2, UGT1A1, VKORC1, CYP4F2, NAT2, G6PD. EXTENDED PANEL (with HLA): adds HLA-A*31:01, HLA-B*15:02, HLA-B*57:01, HLA-B*58:01, ABCG2, COMT, OPRM1, IFNL3, RYR1/CACNA1S. Platform options include targeted genotyping arrays (Illumina GSA + PGx content), clinical sequencing panels (PGx-seq), and whole-genome sequencing with PGx extraction (emerging). Key requirement: CYP2D6 copy number assessment (not achievable by standard SNP arrays alone).
outcomes: Comprehensive 12-gene panel identifies actionable findings in 28-35% of patients; 99% of patients carry at least one actionable variant

title: Return of Pharmacogenomic Results to Patients and Providers
text_chunk: Standardized return of PGx results requires: (1) Machine-readable discrete data in EHR (diplotype, phenotype, activity score stored as structured fields, not PDF attachments); (2) Patient-accessible results via portal with lay-language interpretation; (3) Pharmacist-reviewed clinical summary with actionable recommendations for each drug-gene pair; (4) Lifetime persistence: PGx results do not change (unlike tumor genomics) and should persist in the medical record indefinitely; (5) Portability: HL7 FHIR PGx Implementation Guide enables transfer between health systems; (6) Incidental findings policy: determine approach for variants with non-pharmacogenomic implications (e.g., DPYD and fluoropyrimidine sensitivity may indicate cancer predisposition). CPIC provides standardized phenotype assignment terms and activity score calculations.
outcomes: Structured EHR storage enables 100% CDS alert triggering vs 30% with PDF-only results; patient portal access increases engagement and adherence to PGx recommendations

title: Cost-Effectiveness of Pharmacogenomic Testing
text_chunk: Cost-effectiveness evidence for PGx testing: SINGLE-GENE TESTING: HLA-B*57:01/abacavir: cost-saving across all populations (prevents hospitalization for HSR); HLA-B*15:02/carbamazepine: cost-effective in Asian populations (ICER <$50,000/QALY); DPYD/fluoropyrimidines: cost-saving (prevents ICU admissions for severe toxicity, ~$150 test vs ~$30,000 toxicity hospitalization); CYP2C19/clopidogrel: cost-effective to cost-saving (prevents stent thrombosis, $250-500 test vs $50,000+ MACE treatment). MULTI-GENE PANEL: Pre-emptive 12-gene panel ($250-500) becomes cost-effective after 2+ actionable prescriptions (achieved by most patients by age 65). PREPARE trial showed overall cost savings with panel testing. Barriers to payer coverage include limited RCT evidence for some drug-gene pairs and variable implementation quality.
outcomes: DPYD testing cost-saving at $150/test vs $30,000 avoided toxicity hospitalization; multi-gene panel cost-effective at ICER <$50,000/QALY for most populations

title: Laboratory Standards and Quality Assurance for Pharmacogenomic Testing
text_chunk: Clinical PGx testing requires CLIA certification and CAP accreditation. Key laboratory standards: (1) Validated allele coverage: laboratories must clearly report which star alleles are tested (e.g., CYP2D6 testing must include at minimum *2, *3, *4, *5, *6, *9, *10, *17, *29, *41, and gene duplications); (2) Diplotype assignment: requires phasing algorithms or long-read sequencing for complex genes; (3) Copy number variation: essential for CYP2D6 (deletions, duplications, tandem alleles) using qPCR, MLPA, or digital PCR; (4) Hybrid allele detection: CYP2D6/CYP2D7 hybrid alleles must be distinguished; (5) External quality assessment: participation in CAP PGx proficiency testing surveys; (6) Turnaround time targets: <7 days for pre-emptive, <24 hours for reactive (urgent). The Association for Molecular Pathology (AMP) provides guidelines for PGx variant nomenclature, reporting, and quality metrics.
outcomes: CAP survey concordance for CYP2D6 phenotype assignment: 85-90% (lower for complex structural variants); star allele coverage varies significantly between laboratories

title: Addressing Health Disparities in Pharmacogenomics Implementation
text_chunk: Pharmacogenomic testing panels and algorithms have been developed primarily in European-descent populations, creating potential health equity gaps: (1) Missing alleles: CYP2D6*17, *29, *45 (common in Africans) are absent from many commercial panels, causing PM/IM misclassification as NM; (2) CYP2C9 underrepresentation: *5, *6, *8, *11 alleles (African-predominant) are excluded from most warfarin dosing algorithms (COAG trial showed harm in African Americans); (3) Ancestry-based assumptions: using self-reported race as proxy for allele frequency is imprecise; genotype-first approaches are more accurate; (4) Access disparities: PGx testing is disproportionately accessed by White, insured, academic-center patients. Addressing these gaps requires: inclusive allele panels, diverse validation cohorts, expanded insurance coverage, and community engagement in underserved populations.
outcomes: Population-inclusive panels reduce CYP2D6 misclassification from 15-20% to <5% in African-descent patients; equitable access programs increase PGx testing in Medicaid populations by 3-fold
